BROOKHAVEN – Brookhaven Animal Rescue League is asking the community to help find homes for 33 puppies that recently arrived at the shelter, highlighting what staff say is an ongoing pet overpopulation problem.

According to the rescue league, the puppies came from four mother dogs and include nine “C” puppies, seven “N” puppies, nine “P” puppies and eight “R” puppies, along with one puppy nicknamed “Spot.”

The shelter’s adoption center holds about 50 dogs, making the recent intake a significant strain on available space, the organization said.

Rescue league officials said expanding shelter space is not the answer. Instead, they are encouraging residents to adopt and to support spay and neuter efforts to help prevent more unwanted litters.

“Right now, we need 33 homes for 33 puppies,” the organization said in a social media post.

The puppies are current on vaccinations, microchipped and have been spayed or neutered, with the exception of four that have not yet had surgery, according to the rescue league.

The puppies can be viewed online at barl.net/adopt. In-person visits are available Thursday through Saturday from noon to 3 p.m. The shelter will be closed Easter Sunday.

Those needing an after-hours appointment can contact Gail at 601-757-3211.

Brookhaven Animal Rescue League also reminded pet owners that neutering male dogs is just as important as spaying female dogs in helping reduce pet overpopulation.

HATTIESBURG — Paul B. Johnson State Park has reopened following extensive renovations, with state officials highlighting upgraded campsites, cabins and amenities aimed at improving the visitor experience.

The Mississippi Department of Wildlife, Fisheries and Parks marked the park’s grand reopening March 26 with a public event that included a morning social, a program featuring remarks from state Rep. Larry Byrd and tours of the updated facilities.

The park now features 129 renovated RV campsites equipped with full hookups, including water, electricity and sewer, along with picnic tables and grills.

In addition, officials said the park includes 12 newly renovated cabins and two duplexes. The cabins feature updated kitchens with stainless steel appliances, new dining areas, living room furniture with flatscreen televisions, and upgraded bedrooms and bathrooms with walk-in tile showers. The duplexes also include outdoor porches with picnic tables, fire pits and grills, as well as screened-in back porches with outdoor furniture.

Other improvements at the park include two bathhouses, a day-use restroom, a group camp bathhouse and new air conditioning units in multiple areas.

“The recent renovations at Paul B. Johnson State Park highlights our continued investment in Mississippi State Parks,” said MDWFP Executive Director Lynn Posey. “We are pleased to reopen the park and provide visitors with updated amenities and a chance to explore Mississippi’s great outdoors.”

Reservations for cabins and campsites are now open, according to the agency.

Visitors to the park can take part in activities including fishing, boating and use of a playground, nature trail and disc golf course. Admission is $2 per person, with free entry for children ages 5 and younger.

By Beverly Kraft Administrative Office of Courts

Retired Circuit Judge Robert Helfrich of Hattiesburg died on March 31 at Forrest General Hospital. He was 72.

Funeral arrangements are incomplete.

Judge Helfrich served as Circuit Judge of the 12th Circuit District of Forrest and Perry counties for more than 22 years. He officially retired on June 30, 2025, but continued to work without salary, presiding over the drug intervention court that he created shortly after he took office in 2003.

“He just really made a difference in the judicial system there, and he will be missed,” said retired Circuit Judge Jon Mark Weathers, who served alongside Judge Helfrich for more than eight years.

Judge Helfrich’s legacy includes working tirelessly to turn around the lives of drug addicts whom others had given up on, and righting wrongs committed to preserve segregation in the 1960s.

As an assistant district attorney for the 12th Circuit District, Helfrich reopened and prosecuted racially motivated crimes from the Civil Rights era. He headed the team that prosecuted Ku Klux Klan Imperial Wizard Samuel Bowers in 1998 for ordering the 1966 firebombing death of Vernon F. Dahmer Sr. Dahmer, a Civil Rights activist, successful businessman and farmer, had allowed Blacks to pay poll taxes at his store and had assisted with voter registration.

Hattiesburg attorney Pat Zachary, a longtime friend, said, “Bob was not afraid of anything. He would go back and try old civil rights cases that needed to be tried. He was straight up and brave about it.”

Circuit Judge Wes Curry of Hattiesburg, who came to the Circuit bench a year before Judge Helfrich retired, said, “I was in law school when he was assistant district attorney working on the Vernon Dahmer case, and it really made me proud that I came from a place that sought to do justice for the Dahmer family. He was a primary force in that case. To get to work with him and learn from him was very humbling.”

In 2006, as Circuit Judge, Helfrich ordered exoneration of Clyde Kennard, a Black man who was convicted of burglary involving receipt of stolen chicken feed in September 1960. Kennard had tried repeatedly to enroll in then all-white Mississippi Southern College. His defenders had long argued that Kennard was framed on the burglary charge to prevent him from pursuing college enrollment. He was diagnosed with cancer while serving a seven-year sentence at Parchman. He died in 1963, shortly after being released from prison. The man who testified against him recanted in 2005. After unsuccessful attempts to gain a gubernatorial pardon and Supreme Court vacation of the judgment, 16 people filed a Petition for Exoneration in Forrest County Circuit Court. On May 17, 2006, Judge Helfrich stated at a hearing that he was “compelled to do the right thing, and that is to declare Mr. Kennard innocent and to declare that the conviction of Mr. Kennard is hereby null and void.”

Weathers, who was District Attorney at the time, joined in the motion to exonerate on behalf of the State of Mississippi. Judge Helfrich “just did the right thing and wasn’t worried about the consequences,” he said.

Judge Helfrich was a leader in drug intervention courts. He was among the earliest to create separate tracks for veterans and DUI offenders within drug court. He was appointed in 2009 to the Board of Directors of the National Association of Drug Court Professionals, which later became known as All Rise. He served on the State Intervention Courts Advisory Committee for 12 years.

During his service on the NADCP Board of Directors, he introduced judges and court staff from across the country to some of his court’s innovations to keep participants involved in recovery. One of his early programs was basketball and softball teams for intervention court participants. He said in an interview, “It’s to show them there are things that you can do that are enjoyable that don’t involve the drug of choice.” And it was an opportunity for participants to receive encouragement. He cheered for them while serving as third base coach for the softball team when they played against other teams in Hattiesburg’s intramural league. Their canary yellow athletic shirts sported a “Helfrich’s Heroes” logo.

Judge Helfrich was passionate about saving those addicted to drugs. He accepted people into drug intervention court when others thought they were bound to fail. “He would want to try to save somebody and he thought he could do it,” Weathers said. He didn’t take just the first-time minor offenders. “He said, ‘I want the worst of the worst.’ He saved more of those than I ever thought that he would,” Weathers said.

Circuit Judge T. Michael Reed, who was appointed to the bench after Helfrich retired, said some of his own clients in private practice were accepted into drug intervention court when he didn’t think there was hope for them. “I would think this person is too far gone,” he recalled. Helfrich gave them a chance, and he held them accountable.

Colleagues recalled former intervention court participants who credited Helfrich for saving their lives. Zachary remembered one former intervention court participant who introduced himself at Fieldhouse for the Homeless, where Helfrich and fellow members of Parkway Heights United Methodist Church served breakfast every third Sunday. “He said, ‘You put me in jail because I didn’t mind what you told me in drug court. I needed to go and I don’t think I’d be alive today if it wasn’t for you.’”

Zachary said, “He loved his drug court participants and always wanted to do everything he could for them to keep them out of the prison system.”

Judge Curry said, “There are so many people who came through that drug court. They knew he cared about them and they loved him back…..He made the lives of those who came before him better.”

Weathers said, “It wasn’t just a job for him. It was a passion and it showed.”

He had a really gruff exterior, though.

Zachary recalled introducing Judge Helfrich a few years ago when Helfrich received the Hub Award, an annual honor recognizing individuals for exceptional public service and contributions to the community. Zachary had arranged to have Tootsie Pop candies on each table. “At the end, I compared him to a Tootsie Pop. Bob has a very gruff, tough exterior, but inside he was one of the warmest people and caring people for the underdog.”

The judge also loved dogs, keeping a canine companion with him in the courtroom. Stump, aptly named for his short legs, sat at the judge’s feet or napped on a mat under the bench during court, or slept on the couch in the judge’s office. After Stump passed away, Blaze took his place, accompanying the judge during court proceedings, ceremonies and work in his chambers.

Judge Helfrich was the son of Marjorie B. Helfrich, who was born in Ruleville, Mississippi, and Dutch military pilot Jan Eduard Helfrich. The couple met while both worked at Hawkins Field in Jackson during World War II. Marjorie Helfrich returned to Jackson to raise her six children after Jan Eduard Helfrich passed away.

Judge Helfrich served in the U.S. Coast Guard. He earned his undergraduate degree from George Mason University and his Juris Doctor from the University of Mississippi School of Law. He served as a public defender in Hattiesburg before becoming an assistant district attorney. He was elected to the 12th Circuit Court on Nov. 5, 2002, and took office on Jan. 1, 2003.

The Mississippi Department of Corrections recognized the first graduating class of “The Haven,” a residential rehabilitation program developed within the Mississippi Correctional Institute for Women, during a recent ceremony honoring 23 incarcerated women who completed the program’s initial phase.

“The Haven” is a peer-developed initiative created by incarcerated women to support others working toward personal growth and recovery. The program focuses on addressing challenges such as addiction, unhealthy relationships, and personal accountability, while encouraging participants to pursue long-term positive change.

During opening remarks at the graduation, a long-term incarcerated participant who helped develop the program described its mission: “The Haven was created by incarcerated women for incarcerated women who struggle with habits, hangups, and who are working toward freedom from addiction, bondage, relationships, and finding liberty in Christ.”

The program is structured in three phases, with the first cohort completing Phase One: Refuge. Coursework during this phase includes instruction on emotional awareness, forgiveness, identity, recovery principles, life skills, codependency, and self-discovery. Participants live together in a shared unit, where they attend classes, share meals, and support one another through accountability and peer encouragement.

Dr. Beth Masters, chaplain and facilitator of The Haven program, emphasized the level of commitment required to complete the program. “You have chosen to work on yourself for a season, and that is what it takes. We have dug, and they have really examined themselves in this program. They have received certificates of completion for 11 in-person classes. They were also asked to complete a set of classes on their tablets. They have truly earned these certificates.”

Several participants were also recognized for reaching personal recovery milestones and received sobriety chips to mark their progress.

Graduate Whitney Hixson, an incarcerated individual who has recently been granted parole, shared her personal experience in the program, describing it as a turning point in her life. She noted that The Haven provided a structured, supportive environment where she could reflect, grow, and develop healthier coping strategies. Hixson also spoke about improvements in her relationships and her outlook on the future.

Program leaders emphasized that the initiative is designed to prepare participants for life both during incarceration and after release. “We are equipping women to live outside of this space, whether they are in their freedom outside of the gates or they return to our community,” the inmate facilitator said. “When they leave The Haven, they will carry what they have learned with them and share it with others.”

The program was launched with support from community partners, including First Baptist Church of Jackson, Crossgates Church of Brandon, and God Behind Bars.

MCIW Supt. Katrina Reid commended the graduates for their commitment to the program. “Recovery is a journey of a thousand steps, and today you took a significant one,” Reid said. “The tools you have learned can serve as a strong foundation for continued growth and progress.”

JACKSON – The Mississippi State Department of Health is urging consumers to check their freezers after a public health alert was issued for certain frozen, dinosaur-shaped chicken nuggets that may contain unsafe levels of lead.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Food Safety and Inspection Service issued the alert for 29-ounce bags containing about 36 Great Value Fully Cooked Dino Shaped Chicken Breast Nuggets. The product has a “best if used by” date of Feb. 10, 2027, lot code 0416DPO1215, and establishment number P44164 printed on the back of the bag.

According to FSIS, the nuggets were produced Feb. 10, 2026, and shipped to Walmart stores nationwide.

A recall was not requested because the product is no longer available for sale, but federal officials said they are concerned some bags may still be in consumers’ freezers.

The issue was discovered during routine surveillance sampling conducted by a state partner, according to FSIS.

Health officials warned that lead exposure is especially dangerous for pregnant women, infants and young children because it can harm developing brains and nervous systems and may cause lasting health problems. Officials said there is no safe level of lead exposure and that the amount found in the nuggets could be up to five times higher than the Food and Drug Administration’s interim reference level for children.

Consumers who purchased the product are advised not to eat it and should either throw it away or return it to the store.

FSIS said it is continuing to investigate and that additional products could be added to the alert.

Nettles remains jailed at the Adams County Detention Center.

Mississippi schools and districts will face higher standards for earning accountability grades beginning with the 2025-26 school year, and those grades will establish a new baseline for measuring performance across the state, according to the Mississippi Department of Education.

The department said accountability grades to be released in fall 2026 will not be directly comparable to grades from previous years because of the tougher benchmarks.

As a result, many schools and districts could receive lower letter grades than they earned in 2024-25, even if student performance remains the same or improves on state assessments, the department said.

Mississippi law requires accountability standards to increase when 75% of students are proficient or when 65% of schools or districts earn a grade of B or higher. State officials said that milestone was reached in 2023, when 74% of schools and 71% of districts earned an A or B, compared with 37% for both in 2016.

“Mississippi students and schools have made extraordinary progress, and that progress is exactly why state law requires us to raise the bar,” State Superintendent of Education Lance Evans said in a statement.

The Mississippi Department of Education said it worked for two years with its Accountability Task Force, Technical Advisory Committee and a special Standard Setting Task Force to revise the accountability system. The Mississippi State Board of Education approved the updated standards in November 2025.

Accountability grades are based on multiple measures of student achievement, including statewide assessment results in English language arts, math and science, progress of English learners, performance in advanced courses and career and technical education programs, and graduation rates.

The department said the most significant change for 2025-26 is the higher number of points schools and districts will need to earn each letter grade.

Another change beginning in 2025-26 is the addition of a new Mississippi Readiness Index, which replaces previous college and career readiness measures for high schools and districts. The index includes student performance on the ACT, SAT, ACT WorkKeys and the Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery, as well as success in Advanced Placement, dual credit, dual enrollment and career and technical education programs, industry certifications, diploma endorsements, and on-time and five-year graduation rates.

The department also said the U.S. history assessment will no longer count in accountability measures, and annual goals for English learner progress have been updated.

State assessment results for the 2025-26 school year are expected to be released in August 2026. Accountability grades will follow in fall 2026 and will include a breakdown of the components that make up each school or district’s score.

Evans said families and communities should look beyond the overall letter grade when evaluating school performance under the new system.

STARKVILLE — It’s a long way from Hernando, Mississippi, to Kennedy Space Center, but Matthew Ramsey’s decision to spend a few years in-between the two at Mississippi State University made the trip worth it.

Today, Ramsey is celebrating the success of Wednesday’s launch of NASA’s Artemis II mission—the first crewed mission since 1972—as its mission manager. The 10-day expedition from Earth around the moon marks a major step toward returning humans to the lunar surface and setting the stage for long-term exploration.

The North Mississippi native enrolled at Mississippi State in the early 1990s as a pitcher for the university baseball team while earning a 1992 bachelor’s and 1993 master’s degree in aerospace engineering. He began his work with NASA in 2002.

He said in one of the agency’s website stories, “There are a lot of similarities between mission management and pitching. You control many aspects of the tempo, and there’s a lot of weight on your shoulders.”

On this history-making mission, that responsibility includes pre-launch daily preparations, addressing issues as deputy of the Artemis II management team, and resolving any flight changes.

One of his NASA interview comments about his immeasurable duties was, “Most of my time is focused on making sure we’re ready to fly astronauts Reid, Victor, Christina and Jeremy to the Moon and bring them home safely.”

Also involved with the success of Artemis II is Parker Glass, who works for NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems and has been overseeing budget development, project plans and resource allocation in preparation for Wednesday’s launch.

Glass was exposed to NASA and space exploration during most of his childhood in Yorktown, Virginia, where his dad was employed at Langley Research Center for many years. Glass became enamored with becoming an astronaut, but as he got older his interests changed.

He discovered the prestigious PGA Golf Management program at Mississippi State, one of just 16 in the nation. He said in a NASA article, “I first visited MSU in 2014 and fell in love with Starkville.”

After eventually changing his major to finance, he was surprised to discover there were internship opportunities with NASA and that brought him back to his original passion.

Glass wants students interested in NASA and the agency’s work to know that being an astronaut doesn’t have to factor into the equation of working in space exploration. “NASA needs everybody,” he said.

He graduated from MSU in 2018 with a bachelor’s in business administration and earned a Master of Business Administration degree in 2022.

International students enrich Mississippi College’s culture in a variety of ways, including by sharing unique aspects of their home customs and traditions with their fellow students.

Through captivating presentations and artistic stage performances, the annual International Festival at MC showcases these students’ immense talents.

Sponsored by MC’s International Institute, the 2026 event is scheduled from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. on Thursday, April 9, in Nelson Hall’s Swor Auditorium on the Clinton campus.

Richard Ladner, director of the International Institute, said the festival is the largest international event on campus and the institute’s only performance-oriented program.

“Our students come from a variety of cultures, and they are excited to share their traditions with the people of Mississippi,” Ladner said. “It’s a great opportunity for them to demonstrate artistic endeavors they are passionate about. The audience will have a rare opportunity to see performers from so many countries live and in person. It will be a fantastic night.”

The international students will celebrate aspects of their heritage in three-to-five-minute programs that educate audience members about the fashion, music and customs associated with their respective communities. Proceeds from the festival help support international student scholarships at MC.

Timothy Young, a Master of Accountancy student from Kingston, Jamaica, and an MC track and field athlete who will serve as emcee of this year’s event, said the International Festival highlights the international student population at Mississippi College.

“The International Festival is more than just an event: it is an opportunity for students to share a part of who they are with the campus community,” said Young, who serves as president of the International Student Association at MC. “Events like this help build connections, break down cultural barriers and create a stronger sense of unity among students of all backgrounds.

“My favorite aspect of the festival is the cultural exchange – being able to experience different cultures through traditions and perspectives. It’s an important part of MC’s culture because it highlights and celebrates the diversity of our student body. It reflects MC as a global university.”

As in past festivals, this year’s event will include a crowd-favorite fashion show featuring authentic clothing from a variety of countries, student performances, and guest performers, including dancers from Ballet Magnificat in Jackson and the Southern Pine Singers representing the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in Philadelphia.

“The International Festival is a great way for MC’s international students to continue to forge friendships and relationships with the community,” Ladner added. “It’s also a great way for community members to be exposed to the broader world around them and to witness the broad tapestry of people from different backgrounds at MC.”

Following the festival, audience members will have an opportunity to interact with the performers during a reception in the Nelson Hall lobby. Refreshments will be available.

Tickets to the International Festival cost $10 each for adults, $5 each for students and $25 for families of any size. They may be purchased in advance or at the door. For more information or to purchase tickets, visit mc.edu/international/events/international-festival .

“𝐅𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫, 𝐢𝐟 𝐲𝐨𝐮 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐮𝐩 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐦𝐞; 𝐲𝐞𝐭 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐦𝐲 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐲𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐧𝐞.” — 𝐋𝐮𝐤𝐞 𝟐𝟐:𝟒𝟐

There is a garden in the middle of the worst night in human history. Did you ever think about that? That Jesus was born in a barn and betrayed in a garden? Normal places, but so symbolic. God sure knows how to paint His stories with nuance.

Jesus had just shared a final meal with the people He loved most. He had washed their feet and broken bread and passed the cup and tried to prepare them for something that would level them and they wouldn’t understand until later. And then He walked out into the dark, to a place called Gethsemane.

That garden was at the bottom of the Mount of Olives, and I need you to think about the history there: This is the same mountain where David fled when his son Absalom betrayed him, and the mountain where Zechariah prophesied Jesus would return. It is maybe the most theologically loaded hillside in human history.

Did you know that “Gethsemane” means “oil press?” It’s a mechanism they use to crush olives to produce something valuable. I don’t think that’s a coincidence.

He knelt down, and He prayed such a vulnerable, honest prayer, and He didn’t dress it up. He just fell on His knees in the dirt and in the original language, He called God “אַבָּא,” or “Abba.” That’s a word small children used, equivalent to “daddy” or “papa.”

Essentially, He said, “Dad, if there’s any other way, please. Take this cup from me.”

The Son of the God who spoke the world into existence, the Savior who calmed the sea with His voice, asked His Dad if there was any other way. He felt the weight of what was coming. The physical agony, of course, but also the spiritual and cosmic weight of carrying every sin ever committed by every person who would ever live. Can you imagine? For that time, all the guilt, all the pain, all the temptation and hate and selfishness and longing and all the things that plague our human nature, all of that was HIS. In His most human and desperate and vulnerable moment, the name He reached for was the most intimate one He knew. In His full humanity, He asked His Dad if maybe He wouldn’t have to do this. 𝑃𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑒, 𝐷𝑎𝑑. God said no. Not with words, necessarily, but the cup didn’t pass.

The Bible tells us that God sent an angel, though, not to rescue Him or to reroute the plan, but to strengthen Him for what was ahead. God didn’t remove the suffering. He showed up inside of it. And then Jesus said the bravest thing anyone’s ever said in possibly the worst moment anyone’s ever had: “Not My will, but Yours be done.”

I have prayed some desperate prayers in my life. I’ve been on my knees asking God to change outcomes of the inevitable, to heal people I loved, to reroute plans that felt unbearable. I know some of you reading this are in a place just like that right now. You’re in your own garden, in your own dark night, asking God to please, please find another way.

And sometimes He does. Sometimes the cup moves and the miracle happens and you get to stand there in front of Him with tears streaming down your face in pure gratitude. But sometimes the angel comes to strengthen and comfort instead.

Just like with Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, sometimes God’s answer isn’t deliverance from the fire, but His presence inside it. He doesn’t always pass the cup but sometimes instead gives us the strength to drink it.

And here’s what I’ve learned, more often reluctantly than not: That kind of answer requires more trust than the miracle does. It requires you to loosen your grip on the outcome and really believe that He is good even when the cup is bitter.

Not my will, but yours. Do what’s best here, Dad, no matter what my cost.

That sentence is the hinge all of history swings on, primarily in the garden that night, but also in every moment we face something we didn’t choose and can’t control. It’s the declaration of a faith that has moved past asking God to be our helper and into trusting Him as our Dad.

Jesus made it through Gethsemane. And because He drank that cup all the way to the bottom, Sunday was coming.

But you know what? Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6 both tell us that the Holy Spirit living inside us causes us to cry out, “Abba, Father,” as well. The same word, and the same intimacy. The Apostle Paul is saying in those passages that because of what happened after Gethsemane, because of Jesus’s suffering at the cross and the victory of the resurrection, we as believers are adopted into the same relationship Jesus had with His Dad.

Abba. We get to use that word too. We get to come to God in the dirt on our knees in our worst hour in the dark and call Him Dad and know He hears us.

Whatever garden you’re in right now, whatever cup you’re holding, whatever prayer you’ve prayed that hasn’t moved the mountain yet, He is with you in it. And Sunday is still coming.

Abba, not my will. Yours.

“It’s a shame to kill a defenseless dog who was doing his job to help us keep contraband out of the prison,” Cain said.

Cain noted that killing or injuring a public service animal is a felony in Mississippi, punishable by up to a $5,000 fine, five years in prison, or both.

JACKSON – Attorney General Lynn Fitch, Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi and the Mississippi Department of Child Protection Services are recognizing April as Child Abuse Prevention Month and highlighting a training program designed to strengthen the state’s response to abuse cases.

Fitch, Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi CEO Karla Steckler Tye and Department of Child Protection Services Commissioner Andrea Sanders toured the Child Advocacy Training Institute, a facility that provides hands-on, simulation-based training for students and professionals who may encounter child abuse cases.

State leaders said the institute is intended to help frontline workers better recognize, respond to and prevent child abuse by preparing them for real-world situations in a controlled environment.

“Receiving specialized training on recognizing, responding to, and preventing child abuse is critical for a strong response to child abuse,” Fitch said in a statement. She said the institute helps prepare the workforce that serves as the first line of defense for children experiencing abuse.

Tye said the protection and healing of abused children often depends on how professionals respond in critical moments, and she said the training institute gives them a chance to practice before facing those situations in real life.

Sanders said the facility allows Child Protection Services employees to walk through the full continuum of a case in a realistic, hands-on setting, strengthening how the system responds when abuse is reported.

In addition to touring the institute, Fitch and Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi also shared child safety resources, including a new card offering tips for safe online gaming.

Officials said the card is the third in a series of resources created by the Attorney General’s Office and Children’s Advocacy Centers of Mississippi. April 3 marks National Pony Express Day, a tribute to one of the most legendary and short-lived mail systems in American history.

The Pony Express was a service that played a crucial role in delivering news across a rapidly expanding nation. It’s understandable why we’d like to commemorate one of the first ways people got their long-distance news, and needless to say, it was a lot more dangerous back then. Breaking news was slower, but much harder-fought than it is now.

According to NationalToday.com, today we honor the founders and fearless riders of the mail delivery system on horseback that revolutionized communication in the early 1860s. Beyond letters, the service became a vital pipeline for newspapers and breaking news, helping keep the East and West informed at a time when the country was on the brink of the Civil War.

The Pony Express officially began operations on April 3, 1860, at a time when the country lacked a fast, reliable way to send messages across vast distances. NationalToday.com says the service emerged in response to California’s population surge during the Gold Rush, when prospectors, investors and businesses needed quicker communication with the East.

According to Britannica.com, the demand for faster delivery was driven in part by the need for timely news, as existing methods could take weeks. With tensions rising ahead of the Civil War, rapid transmission of information became increasingly important, making the Pony Express an essential link for newspapers and businesses trying to stay current.

The system was founded by freighting entrepreneurs Alexander Majors, William Russell and William B. Waddell, operating under the name Central Overland California and Pikes Peak Express Company. At its peak, the operation employed thousands and used extensive infrastructure, including horses, relay stations and supply networks, to move mail across the frontier, according to NationalToday.com.

What made the Pony Express remarkable was its speed. Messages that once took weeks or months to reach the West Coast could now be delivered in about 10 days. NationalToday.com notes one famous delivery, carrying President Abraham Lincoln’s inaugural address, arrived in just seven days and 17 hours.

According to Britannica.com, the Pony Express relied on a relay system of riders traveling a nearly 2,000-mile route from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California, with mail continuing to San Francisco by steamer. Riders typically covered 75 to 100 miles each, switching horses every 10 to 15 miles at roughly 190 stations scattered across rugged terrain.

The service was both efficient and dangerous. Britannica.com says riders faced harsh weather, difficult landscapes and threats of attack, yet the system lost only one bag of mail during its 18 months of operation. (That feels a little more reliable than now, doesn’t it?) Young, lightweight riders were preferred to maximize speed, and many became folk heroes of the American West.

Among them were figures like William “Buffalo Bill” Cody and Robert “Pony Bob” Haslam, whose endurance and daring helped cement the Pony Express in American folklore. Britannica.com notes that their exploits captured the national imagination and made the service one of the most colorful chapters in Western history.

Despite its success in speed and reliability, the Pony Express was financially unsustainable. NationalToday.com reports the company struggled with mounting costs and ultimately shut down on Oct. 24, 1861, just as the transcontinental telegraph made near-instant communication possible.

Britannica.com adds that the telegraph’s completion rendered the service obsolete, bringing an abrupt end to the Pony Express after just 18 months. Still, its impact was lasting.

The Pony Express helped pave the way for a unified, year-round transcontinental communication system, influencing how information and goods moved across the country.

Today, National Pony Express Day serves as a reminder of the ingenuity and grit that defined an era, and of the riders who raced against time to deliver not just mail, but the news that kept a growing nation connected.

TUPELO — The National Park Service on Friday released a report detailing environmental conditions and proposed cleanup options for the former Ridgeland Firing Range along the Natchez Trace Parkway, opening a 30-day public comment period.

The report, known as an Engineering Evaluation/Cost Analysis, outlines possible contamination at the site and presents a recommended plan for addressing it. An accompanying administrative record file includes documents and data used to develop the report.

The firing range operated from 1984 to 2002 in Ridgeland. The National Park Service is addressing the site under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act, a federal law governing the cleanup of hazardous substances.

According to the agency, the report evaluates the nature and extent of contamination, potential risks to public health and the environment, and possible cleanup alternatives. The effort is being conducted as a non-time critical removal action, meaning officials have at least six months to plan before cleanup activities begin.

The public can review the report and administrative record online at parkplanning.nps.gov/RidgelandRange or in person at the Natchez Trace Parkway Visitor Center, 2680 Natchez Trace Parkway in Tupelo, during regular business hours Monday through Friday.

Comments will be accepted from April 3 through May 3 and can be submitted through the project website. Requests to extend the comment period by 15 days must be submitted before May 3 via email to [email protected] .

All comments will become part of the public record. While commenters may request that personal identifying information be withheld, the National Park Service said it cannot guarantee confidentiality.

Officials said the department’s investigations division continues to look into the cases, but deputies are emphasizing prevention in hopes of stopping the crimes before more people lose money.

According to the sheriff’s department, scammers are becoming increasingly convincing and are making themselves appear more legitimate than in the past. Deputies said some scammers are now using existing business email addresses, websites and phone numbers to make their schemes seem real.

The department urged anyone who suspects they may be dealing with a scam to hang up and contact local law enforcement before responding further.

Officials said residents should tell law enforcement what the caller or sender is saying and ask whether the situation appears to be a scam.

April Fools’ Day, celebrated on April 1st each year, has a history shrouded in folklore. While the exact origins of this playful day are unclear, there are several theories that attempt to explain its inception.

One popular theory traces the tradition back to the change from the Julian calendar to the Gregorian calendar in the late 16th century when New Year’s Day moved from the end of March to January 1st. Those who continued to celebrate the New Year in April were labeled as fools and became the subjects of pranks and jokes.

Another theory links April Fools’ Day to ancient Roman and Celtic festivities that marked the arrival of spring with lighthearted pranks and mischievous behavior. Some even suggest a connection to the Roman festival of Hilaria, a day of laughter and jokes celebrated at the end of March.

The purpose of April Fools’ Day is to embrace lighthearted humor and playfulness, allowing people to engage in (hopefully harmless) pranks and jokes. It serves as a day to step away from the seriousness of everyday life and to share laughter with friends and family. The tradition of playing pranks on April 1st lets us spread a little joy and humor in a world that often needs a moment of levity.
